A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Factored-NeuS and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The shared methods and experiments can be matched despite extensive reorganization. v1 has no separate appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original reconstruction and inverse-rendering experiments on DTU, SK3D, Shiny, and IndiSG, including quantitative results and component ablations.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F retain original experiments and add Glossy evaluations, broader DTU results, additional baseline comparisons, and controlled ablations.

M1.justification: The core three-stage pipeline and principal losses remain. Appendix F.2 adds an evaluated adaptation incorporating Geo-NeuS point-cloud and image-pair supervision. Stage 3 also describes the BRDF as Ward rather than Disney; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an implementation change or a corrected description.

E1.justification: v2 adds the 13-scene Glossy benchmark, covering real and synthetic reflective objects, and extends DTU evaluation from four glossy scenes to 15 scenes including regular objects. Figure 22 additionally evaluates relighting under changed illumination. The original four datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: NeRO is added to existing geometry comparisons and IndiSG material comparisons. Ref-NeuS, previously only discussed, is evaluated in Figure 7. Figures 9 and 25 introduce UniSDF and Ref-NeRF/S3-NeRF-based architectural comparisons. Original principal baselines remain; Figure 18's inconsistent replacement labels do not establish additional material-baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: Added controlled experiments introduce auxiliary SfM point-cloud/image-pair supervision and a Fresnel comparison of 0.02 versus 0.75, alongside an indirect-illumination removal condition. The retained evaluations preserve Chamfer distance, foreground PSNR, and the reported 300K/40K training budgets. Newly disclosed default settings are distinguished from these experimental interventions.

E4.justification: v2 adds indirect-light removal tests, auxiliary-supervision comparisons, rendering-architecture alternatives, and Fresnel sensitivity analysis (Table 3, Table 7, Figures 9 and 24–26). Figure 13 extends surface-reconstruction ablations to additional objects. The original specular-albedo, visibility, and surface-component ablations remain, including relocated or renamed presentations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Reported means aggregate scene results rather than repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Many quantitative and qualitative results are added, while matched entries from v1 Tables 2–4 remain unchanged in v2 Tables 1, 3, and 4. New results include a 15-scene DTU mean Chamfer distance of 0.76 versus NeuS's 0.83, and a Glossy mean of 0.0044 versus NeRO's 0.0033. Additional results document indirect-light, supervision, architecture, and Fresnel effects.

T1.justification: Appendix E, Equation 27, newly specifies the visibility–Spherical Gaussian approximation through illumination-weighted visibility scaling of the lobe amplitude, previously left implicit in the product notation. Most earlier rendering and loss equations are retained or relocated. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: v2 explicitly limits its stated research scope to implicit representations, distinguishing the contribution from Gaussian-splatting approaches. The central claims of image-only, three-stage glossy-object reconstruction and superior geometry/material reconstruction remain. Its stronger emphasis on joint surface and volume rendering describes a component already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 proposes model complexity and training instability as explanations for specular-albedo-related lighting degradation, clarifies that Stage 1 colors are not a physical BRDF, and discusses Fresnel-versus-texture tradeoffs. Appendix G explains limited DTU97 gains through the small proportion of glossy regions, replacing v1's broader smooth-surface restriction while retaining fine-detail limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices B and E newly disclose grayscale Stage 1 specular radiance, NeRF++ background modeling, the default Fresnel value, the Glossy loss weight, and 32 visibility-sampling directions. Architecture, schedules, hardware, and training-time information largely remain. Conversely, v1's explicit image resolutions and several view/train/test counts are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates the research context through discussion of Gaussian-splatting reconstruction and inverse rendering, explicitly motivating continued work on implicit representations. It adds NeRO, UniSDF, S3-NeRF, Ward, and other references with substantive connections to the method and comparisons. The earlier capabilities survey table is removed.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially condensed and revised. Preliminaries, implementation details, detailed training equations, Stage 2 explanations, and limitations move into organized appendices, while the main method and experimental narrative are restructured. Ablation terminology and author/header information also change.

P2.justification: The opening figures are merged, the pipeline diagram gains Stage 2, existing comparison grids are split or relocated, and numerous new figures and tables are introduced. Table ordering, highlighting, and page layout change extensively. Some edits introduce errors: Figure 3's caption reverses dataset sides, and Figure 18 assigns inconsistent method labels to retained material panels.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central glossy-reconstruction claims through relevant reflective-object baselines, the Glossy benchmark, regular DTU scenes, and targeted component and sensitivity tests. The new evidence also exposes a boundary: NeRO performs better on Glossy overall. These gains address important comparison and generalization gaps in v1 and outweigh the loss of some dataset details and newly introduced figure-label/reference errors, although those errors reduce clarity and reproducibility.
